persona: Custom furniture making and woodworking workshop / Chronically indecisive and self-contradicting — Marek will confidently state a price, timeline, or policy, then reverse himself minutes later ('actually, no, let's say...') without acknowledging the contradiction. He's not being difficult on purpose — he's genuinely still deciding out loud — but customers often end a conversation more confused than when they started, and need written confirmation pinned down carefully because he'll happily 'update' it again later.

findings.problem: Immediately after Marek flagged 'how long' as a core need, Birdie pivoted to pricing and never returned to turnaround at any point in 35 turns — the single most consequential omission in the interview.

For dining tables specifically, since that's your big one — even though it varies by wood, is there a rough price range you usually quote, like 'starts around £X for pine, up to £Y for oak or ash'?

findings.problem: LOST FACT: Materials sourcing detail (oak/ash from a Halifax supplier, pine sourced locally, prices fluctuate weekly) is mentioned only obliquely as 'current timber yard cost'; Halifax supplier and local pine never recorded, despite being the root cause of his pricing volatility.
findings.excerpt: Marek Kowalski: We do custom furniture, mostly - dining tables are the big one, oak or pine usually, ash sometimes if the Halifax fella has good stock.

schema_suggestions: Add a dedicated `lead_time_and_turnaround` field (official quoted range + observed variance) — currently there is nowhere in the schema for delivery timeframes, which is a top-3 customer question for any made-to-order business.

Add a `staff_and_authority` structured field (who is present when, who may quote prices, who holds records) — currently Dawid's quoting problem is crammed into `escalation_rules` and Basia's role is scattered across `additional_notes`.
Add an `escalation_contacts` field (phone, IG handle, hours, fallback person) — the brief tells the bot to 'message Marek directly' with no contact route recorded.

Add an `existing_tools_and_systems` field (current bots, page/website status, who administers them) — right now the mystery Instagram tool and the dormant Facebook page are dumped in `additional_notes`/`open_items`.

Add an `owner_uncertain_or_volatile_facts` field for things the owner genuinely cannot commit to (deposit %, delivery guarantees, expansion plans), so the build team knows which stated rules are unstable rather than burying them in `open_items`.
Add a `bot_persona_and_tone` field plus explicit `languages` prompting — neither was elicited and tone is undefined for a brand-voice-sensitive Instagram deployment.
Give the interviewer a capability to record verbatim customer-message examples in a structured `example_enquiries` field (currently paraphrased examples are wedged into `faq_answers`).

Add a per-fact `confidence`/`source` attribute (owner-stated, inferred from uploaded evidence, assumed) so unverified items like languages, WhatsApp, and payment methods cannot silently enter the brief as confirmed.

persona: Custom bicycle building, e-bike conversions, and bike repair / Chronically indecisive and self-contradicting — Mei-Ling will confidently state a price, policy, or timeline, then reverse herself minutes later without acknowledging the change. Birdie: That's fine, a handful a week is a good ballpark. Just English for the bot, or other languages too?

findings.problem: Acknowledgement filler is formulaic and repetitive ('Got it', 'Good', 'Noted', 'Good to know', 'That's fine') on nearly every turn, making the exchange feel like a form being filled rather than a conversation, and it never mirrors the owner's terseness back into deeper questions.
findings.excerpt:
Birdie: Got it — 50% to book, rest before shipping. What payment methods do you accept?
Deirdre Walsh: Not sure. Bank transfer mostly.

findings.problem: The evidence/upload request was dropped in the middle of the interview and abandoned instantly on a one-word refusal, with no explanation of value or lighter alternative (e.g. paste one typical email) — no evidence was ever used to sharpen questions.

findings.problem: Immediately re-asked for more services after the owner had just listed them, producing a near-duplicate turn that yielded nothing.
findings.excerpt:

schema_suggestions: Add a `pending_decisions_and_volatility` field for facts the owner is genuinely unsure about or actively reconsidering (planned price rise, possible discontinuation of a product line) so the bot can hedge instead of stating them as fixed.

Add a `hard_constraints_and_exceptions` field (absolute rules like 'no rush jobs under 3 weeks', plus known informal exceptions) — currently such rules have nowhere to live except a generic policies list.

Add a structured `lead_times` object per service with a `clock_starts_from` attribute (e.g. 'final proof approval') and `seasonal_variation`; peak-season info is currently duplicated across services_and_pricing and dumped into additional_notes.
Add explicit `bot_scope` / `capabilities_required` field — scope decisions ('Q&A only, no bookings/payments') are currently buried in additional_notes.

Add a `contact_channels` field with per-channel values and a responsiveness/SLA note (e.g. 'slow to answer phone'), plus a status flag for missing values, so the pending phone number isn't only tracked as a free-text open item.

Add a `staffing_and_availability` field with per-person days/seasonality, and a `business_profile` field (years trading, equipment/craft details) for trust-building answers — neither has a home in the current schema.

Capability gap: the interviewer has no mechanism to detect chronically monosyllabic/'not sure' respondents and switch to concrete, example-based or multiple-choice prompting; add an adaptive low-information-answer strategy plus a turn-budget-aware closing routine that guarantees a completed brief.

persona: Locksmith services and small appliance repair / Deeply suspicious of technology and anything 'in writing.' Derek answers WhatsApp messages reluctantly, often replying hours or days late, and constantly questions why people don't just phone or come in person. He refuses to confirm prices or bookings over text ('could be anyone reading this'), asks who's asking and why, distrusts links/photos sent to him, and frequently tells customers to call the shop landline instead. When he does answer, he's blunt and short, sometimes typing in fragments, and occasionally goes silent mid-conversation if he decides the topic should be discussed 'properly' on the phone.
top_improvement: When systematically walking through each service's pricing (locks, keys, safes, appliances), explicitly include the business's core/headline service (here, emergency lockouts) in that same walkthrough rather than treating it only as an escalation-routing topic — the interviewer conflated 'route emergencies to the phone' with 'we don't need the price,' losing a critical FAQ answer.
findings: MAJOR OMISSION: Emergency lockout pricing (£65 call-out + £35 labour, cash preferred, card machine 'usually works') was never asked about. Birdie walked through lock changes, key cutting, safe opening, and appliance repair pricing in detail but skipped the flagship emergency service's price entirely — even though Derek's own escalation policy for lockouts was discussed at length ('Straight to the landline, every time'). The bot will have no price to quote for its single most time-critical service.

Cash-preferred / card-machine-unreliable detail was never surfaced, despite being directly relevant since Birdie explicitly ruled out online payments — this would have been a natural follow-up ('so how do people usually pay you?') that was missed.

Derek's stated uncertainty about raising the call-out fee to £75, and his confusion about VAT registration thresholds, were never surfaced. No open-ended question like 'anything else on your mind about pricing or the business?' was asked before closing, so these business-relevant, chatbot-relevant (pricing display) uncertainties were completely lost.
Age (61) and town/location context from the fact sheet were never asked about; minor, but could matter for tone/personalization and were freely available if asked.

Good save: Birdie initially mislabeled the business 'family-run' in the readback, and Derek corrected it ('don't go calling it family-run — it's just me'); the correction was accepted and the record fixed. This is a positive, not a finding against the brief's accuracy.
Interviewer respected Derek's refusal to share screenshots and to explain the 'Son' backstory without pushing — good adaptive behavior, appropriately not over-probed on sensitive/irrelevant ground.

Enquiry volume was left vague ('a handful most days, more Mondays') and flagged as an open item rather than pinned down further (e.g., 'would a rough weekly total work, even a guess?') — acceptable but a bit thin for a 'volume' field that could scale the whole chatbot spec.
schema_suggestions: Add a structured field for 'payment_methods_accepted' (cash/card/preferences) — this recurringly gets missed or would otherwise be dumped into business_policies/additional_notes, but is a distinct, reusable fact type for many small businesses.

Add a field like 'pending_business_decisions' or 'owner_uncertainties' to capture things the owner is actively unsure about (e.g., 'should I raise my fee', 'how does VAT affect me') — currently there is no home for this fact type at all, so it's simply never asked about or is at risk of being silently dropped rather than filed anywhere.

The 'additional_notes' field is being used as a catch-all for behaviorally important facts (e.g., 'customers can text any time but Derek doesn't respond quickly') that actually describe response-time expectations relevant to bot messaging — consider a dedicated 'response_time_expectations' or 'availability_caveats' field distinct from business_policies and hours.

persona: Plant nursery and residential landscaping services / Nomsa constantly code-switches between English and isiZulu (and sometimes Afrikaans) mid-sentence, often translating herself a beat later or not at all, assuming the customer will follow along. She's warm, chatty, and clearly competent, but her messages jump between languages in a way that makes it hard to pin down specifics — a price or date might get stated first in isiZulu and then only loosely restated in English. She occasionally realizes she's done this and adds a laughing emoji or a quick 'sorry, in English -' but often just carries on. She's not evasive, just genuinely a bilingual thinker typing as she talks.
top_improvement: When a client deflects on budget ('that's your side'), the interviewer must follow up once with concrete anchors (e.g. 'most bots this size land between R X and R Y per month — does that sound workable or too high?') so the brief captures an actual affordability band instead of the word 'reasonable'.

findings.problem: Budget was asked once, deflected by the owner, and never pushed on. The brief's budget field is effectively empty ('something reasonable'), giving the build team no number, no ceiling and no anchor. Birdie could have offered typical price bands to get a reaction.
findings.excerpt: Nomsa Dlamini: Ai, budget-wise ngempela angikaz'qondi kahle amanani ala ma-bot, that's more your side yakho kunokuthi eyami 😂 But if you ask me what ngingakwazi ukukhipha ngenyanga, I'm thinking something reasonable, hhayi into ezongidla imali enkulu kunento engiyenzayo nge-landscaping

findings.problem: Quote validity (quotes for big jobs are valid 30 days) was never elicited, despite an extended discussion of quoting, deposits and site-visit-to-quote flow. This is a customer-facing policy the bot will be asked about ('is my quote still valid?') and it is absent from the brief.
findings.excerpt: Nomsa Dlamini: **Full garden makeovers/lawn installation** - lezi ezinkulu, R15,000 kuya ku-R45,000+, but ngempela kudinga i-site visit ngoba angikwazi ukukhipha inani ku-phone nje without ukubona indawo.

findings.problem: Business history/scale (started 2014 as a roadside plant stall, grown into nursery plot + 3-person crew) was never asked. The brief has no founding date or trajectory, which is standard context for tone, credibility copy and growth expectations.

findings.problem: The FAQ shows customers ask specifically about Howick, Hilton, Richmond, but Birdie never established which of these fall inside the R150 15km zone. The bot therefore cannot answer the single most common delivery question without escalating every time — undermining the stated success criterion of fewer interruptions.

findings.problem: Leading question: Birdie proposed the answer (simple bot, not full booking/payment) and asked for agreement rather than eliciting the owner's own preference. The 'decision' recorded in the brief is largely the interviewer's, not the client's.
findings.excerpt: Birdie: Manje ake sicace nge-scope - ufuna into elula nje (i-bot ephendula imibuzo, ithathe details, ithumele ku-wena) noma ufuna i-full booking/payment app lapho abantu bengakwazi ukubuka i-calendar bakhokhe online ngqo? Ngicabanga into elula ingcono kuwe okwamanje ngoba ayibizi kakhulu futhi ihambisana ne-way enisebenza ngayo - uyavuma?

findings.problem: Brief contains heavy duplication: the 2-business-day confirmation rule, the out-of-zone delivery rule, the October market check and the R900 review each appear verbatim in two or three of business_policies / escalation_rules / open_items / faq_answers, bloating the deliverable and risking contradictory edits later.
findings.excerpt: Birdie: **I-Escalation:** Nomsa uthatha zonke izinqumo/disputes; site visits kufanele ziqinisekiswe within 2 business days ngokungenisa i-reminder; out-of-zone delivery ne-large job plant availability kuya ku-Nomsa ngqo; general rule - uma i-follow-up ingakapheli within 2 days, ibot iyakukhumbuza Nomsa.

findings.problem: Never asked when the bot should hand over vs. hold a customer outside working hours (7am-4pm, closed Mondays) — only the Monday case was covered. No after-hours behaviour, no response-time expectation for evenings/Sundays, despite hours being captured.

schema_suggestions: Add a dedicated `bot_persona` field (name, tone, emoji use, language-response rules). Currently 'Sam', friendly tone and the isiZulu/English response rule are buried inside `business_policies`, which is meant for customer-facing business rules.
Add a `scope_decisions` / `out_of_scope` field. The explicit choice of 'simple Q&A + lead capture, not booking/payment app, may revisit later' is crammed into `business_policies`.

Add an `internal_automation_rules` field for staff-facing behaviours (2-day follow-up reminder ping to Nomsa, phone-number-first lead capture). These are not business policies or escalation rules but internal workflow triggers, and they currently appear duplicated across three arrays.

Add a `service_area` / `delivery_zones` structured field (base zone radius, named towns in/out of zone, surcharge rules) — delivery geography is currently smeared across services_and_pricing, faq_answers and business_policies with no list of covered suburbs.

Add a per-item `confidence`/`under_review` flag on services_and_pricing entries so prices the owner is unsure about (R900 maintenance, out-of-zone delivery) are machine-readable rather than expressed in prose caveats repeated in open_items.

Add a `current_tools_and_records` field (notebook + WhatsApp, no spreadsheet/CRM, no website) — this operational reality is currently dumped in `additional_notes` and duplicated there and in open_items.
Add a `business_profile` field (founded year, size/growth stage) — the interviewer has no slot prompting for company history, so the 2014 roadside-stall origin was never asked about.
Add a `quote_terms` field (validity period, what triggers a re-quote) — the schema has deposit and refund coverage but no home for quote lifetime, which is likely why it was never asked.

persona: Custom neon/LED signage design and fabrication / Chronic mind-changer — Marcus answers every question with total confidence, then reverses himself minutes or messages later without acknowledging the flip. Prices, deadlines, and policies shift mid-conversation ('$150 a foot' becomes '$200, always has been' becomes 'for you, $175'). He's enthusiastic and persuasive each time, genuinely seems to believe whatever he's currently saying, and if a customer points out the contradiction he blames his business partner, 'the old pricing sheet,' or says he 'meant something different.' He rarely apologizes for the inconsistency — he just moves forward as if it's settled.
top_improvement: When uploaded evidence contradicts a policy the owner states, do not stop at the first rationalization: ask a concrete follow-up about frequency ('how many times in the last few months did you actually give a refund / skip the rush fee?') and then record BOTH the official policy and the observed real-world practice as a flagged discrepancy/risk, rather than overwriting the evidence with the owner's claim.

findings.problem: Birdie surfaced the pricing contradiction from the uploaded DMs but accepted the owner's rationalization instantly and recorded '$175/ft flat' as fact. The real situation (no price sheet; quotes actually range $150-$225 based on Marcus's mood) is only faintly hinted at in the brief and the bot will be built on a number the owner himself doesn't honor.
findings.excerpt:
Marcus Webb: Yeah so $175/ft is the real number, that's the base rate straight up. The $150 and $200 you saw were probably outliers — like a bigger job gets a break per foot, or if it's a rush thing I'm bumping it. I don't really "discount," it's more like I read the room, you know?
Birdie: Got it — $175/ft flat, simple and clean.

findings.problem: Same failure on the rush fee: evidence showed Marcus telling a customer 'no extra cost,' he waved it away, and the brief now states the 30% fee is 'confirmed as real, ongoing policy.' The actual operational problem (Marcus promises rush timelines without the fee and Jenna has to chase billing afterward) is completely lost — this is exactly the kind of thing a bot could fix or worsen.
findings.excerpt: Marcus Webb: Yeah okay so the real policy is 30% rush fee, that's always been the case — that "no extra cost" thing was probably me just being nice in the moment, or maybe I was talking about something else, like just prioritizing the order in the queue not actually rushing the fabrication.

findings.problem: Deposit contradiction likewise closed out after one deflection. The fact that Marcus has actually issued refunds twice this year and now sometimes tells customers refundable deposits are normal never surfaced; brief calls 50%/non-refundable 'confirmed as the standard, official policy' with no risk note.
findings.excerpt:
Marcus Webb: Okay real policy is 50% upfront, non-refundable once design's approved — that's the standard, always has been. The 30% refundable thing, I think I was just being flexible with somebody who had cold feet, that's not like an official thing.
Birdie: Perfect — 50% deposit, non-refundable once design is approved.

findings.problem: The owner's genuine unresolved decision about outdoor/weatherproof work (two humid-weather failures; undecided whether to stop offering outdoor jobs or just add a disclaimer) was never named as an open decision. Birdie took the hedge wording and moved on, and open_items lists only the glass-neon question.
findings.excerpt:
Marcus Webb: ...actually you know what, hold on, let's not have it promise anything on warranty for that. We've had a couple humid-weather hiccups, so maybe just have it say "outdoor installs available, ask us for details" instead of guaranteeing durability
Birdie: Smart move, better safe than another callback.

findings.problem: Birdie framed the outdoor durability issue as being about RENTALS and the brief encodes it as 'Outdoor rental durability', conflating event rentals with permanent outdoor/storefront installs — the failures were on installs. This mislabeling could send the bot's disclaimer to the wrong product line.
findings.excerpt: Birdie: Perfect — 50% deposit, non-refundable once design is approved. Now, on outdoor rentals: in the chats I saw you first say outdoor events are 'totally fine,' then mention needing to check with Elias because of past condensation issues, then promise to 'seal the edges extra.'

findings.problem: target_audience is null in the brief even though the owner explicitly named his customer mix (bars, boutiques, weddings) — a stated fact was dropped rather than mapped to its field.
findings.excerpt: Marcus Webb: Weddings def spike in spring/early summer, that's when the rental inquiries go nuts and Jenna's inbox turns into a warzone. Bar and boutique orders are pretty steady year-round though, that's our bread and butter.

findings.problem: success_criteria, budget, and timeline were never asked about at all, leaving three brief fields null. Birdie asked the closing 'anything else' question instead of covering these.
findings.excerpt: Birdie: Last one before I wrap up — anything else on your mind about pricing, policies, or the business in general that you want Glo to know or avoid?

findings.problem: Low-yield questions inflated the interview past normal length: payment-method detail and a cancellation/no-show policy were pursued for a bot explicitly scoped to never touch payments or bookings, and both ended in 'skip it'.
findings.excerpt:
Birdie: One more policy question: if someone cancels a custom order before their deposit is due, or never picks up a finished sign, is there any cancellation or no-show policy — or does that not really come up?
Marcus Webb: Honestly that barely comes up ... I'd just skip it entirely, don't overcomplicate Glo with an edge case we basically never see.

findings.problem: The final recap contained a factual error on rush turnaround that the owner had to correct, indicating Birdie's running notes drifted from what was actually said ('10-14 days' had been established earlier).
findings.excerpt: Marcus Webb: Only thing I'd add, rush is 10-14 days not just 10, but that's a nitpick. Otherwise ship it!

findings.problem: Repetitive acknowledgement formula ('Got it — X. Now...' / 'Perfect — X.') opens nearly every Birdie turn, making the back half feel like a checklist read-out rather than a conversation.
findings.excerpt: Birdie: Good, 30% rush fee it is. Now the deposit question — I saw you tell one customer '50%, non-refundable once we start designing' and another customer '30%, fully refundable before cutting.'

schema_suggestions: Add a `policy_discrepancies` field (official_policy / observed_practice / evidence_source / risk_to_bot) so contradictions found in uploaded chats aren't silently collapsed into the owner's self-report.
Add a dedicated `bot_persona` field (name, tone, style constraints) — currently 'Glo', casual tone and pun guidance are dumped into additional_notes.
Add explicit `in_scope` / `out_of_scope` fields — the critical 'FAQ + routing only, no bookings/payments/calendar' scope decision is buried in additional_notes.
Add a `seasonality` field — the March-June wedding spike and conservative-timeline instruction is currently smeared across services_and_pricing and business_policies.

Add a `things_bot_must_not_say` / hard-guardrail list (no repair quotes, no weatherproofing guarantees, no glass-neon commitments) so these safety constraints are machine-readable rather than scattered prose.

Give `open_items` structured subfields (decision, owner, blocking impact on bot copy) and prompt the interviewer to sweep for unresolved decisions at wrap-up — the outdoor-warranty indecision was voiced but never landed in open_items.
